objective_for_doctor: Assess and manage a patient presenting with epigastric discomfort and cramping pain.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Doctor: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today? Patient: I’ve had epigastric discomfort and cramping pain for the past two hours, and this feels similar to episodes I’ve had before, mostly after meals. It usually eases a few hours after eating, but I’ve been avoiding food and I’ve lost some weight over the last couple of months.
Is the pain typically worse right after you eat, or does it get worse when you haven't eaten for several hours (like before meals or at night)?
It’s typically worse right after I eat, and it tends to ease after a few hours. I don’t notice it being worse when I haven’t eaten for several hours or at night.
Have you been experiencing nausea or vomiting, and if so, does the vomit contain undigested food or appear coffee-ground in color?

I haven’t had any nausea or vomiting, and I haven’t noticed any coffee-ground or undigested-food appearance. My main issue is the cramping epigastric discomfort that starts after eating and then improves after a few hours.
Does the pain radiate to your back, right shoulder, or right upper quadrant, or does it stay confined to the epigastric area?
Patient: It stays mostly in the epigastric area and doesn’t really radiate to my back, right shoulder, or right upper quadrant.
Do you feel full quickly when eating (early satiety), or do you get the pain even with small amounts of food?
Patient: I do feel pretty full quickly when I try to eat, and the pain can still come on even with smaller amounts. It generally starts after I eat, then eases a few hours later.
Have you noticed any black, tarry stools, or any blood in your stool?
Patient: I haven’t noticed any black, tarry stools or any blood in my stool. I haven’t had any changes in my bowel habits either.
Have you been taking any medications regularly, particularly ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, or other anti-inflammatory drugs?
I’ve been taking over-the-counter painkillers for my chronic knee pain, mostly around that time—sometimes ibuprofen or similar anti-inflammatory medicines. I don’t take aspirin regularly.
How old are you, and approximately how much weight have you lost over the past couple of months?
I’m 38 years old, and I’ve lost about 10 to 15 pounds over the past couple of months because I’ve been avoiding eating.
Do you ever wake up at night with this pain, or does it strictly occur after eating during the day?
It doesn’t really wake me up at night—the pain is mainly after meals during the day. I don’t notice it being worse when I haven’t eaten for several hours.
Have you tried antacids or acid-reducing medications (like famotidine or omeprazole), and if so, do they provide any relief?
Patient: I haven’t tried antacids or anything like omeprazole or famotidine yet, so I’m not sure if they’d help—I’ve just been avoiding eating because the pain comes after meals.
Do you have any difficulty swallowing food, or does it feel like food gets stuck when you eat?
No, I don’t have trouble swallowing and nothing feels like it gets stuck when I eat. It’s mostly the cramping epigastric discomfort that starts after I eat and then improves after a few hours.
Do you have any personal history of H. pylori infection, or any family history of stomach cancer or ulcers?
I don’t know of any prior H. pylori infection, and I haven’t been told I have ulcers. I don’t have any known family history of stomach cancer or ulcers.
Do you drink alcohol, and if so, how much and how often?
Patient: I drink alcohol only occasionally—maybe a few drinks on weekends, but not daily. I haven’t increased my alcohol intake recently.

Have you noticed any abdominal bloating or visible swelling after meals, or any fever?

[DDX] NSAID-induced gastric ulcer, NSAID-induced gastritis, functional dyspepsia, gastric outlet obstruction (partial), gastric malignancy
